qns_content.text: A copper block of dimensions \( 0.4 \, \text{m} \times 0.2 \, \text{m} \times 0.05 \, \text{m} \) is subjected to a shearing force of \( 1.5 \times 10^4 \, \text{N} \). If the shear modulus of copper is \( 4.2 \times 10^{10} \, \text{N/m}^2 \), what is the shear strain?

text_solutions:
Shear modulus: \( G = \frac{\text{Shear stress}}{\text{Shear strain}} \).

Shear stress: \( \text{Shear stress} = \frac{F}{A} \), \( A = 0.4 \times 0.2 = 0.08 \, \text{m}^2 \).

Shear stress: \( \frac{1.5 \times 10^4}{0.08} = 1.875 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/m}^2 \).

Shear strain: \( \text{Shear strain} = \frac{\text{Shear stress}}{G} = \frac{1.875 \times 10^5}{4.2 \times 10^{10}} \approx 4.46 \times 10^{-6} \).

qns_content.text: What does the term "elastic limit" refer to in the context of a material’s stress-strain behavior?

options.text: The maximum stress before plastic deformation begins
The maximum stress beyond which the material does not return to its original shape
The minimum stress required for permanent deformation

text_solutions: The elastic limit is the maximum stress a material can withstand while still returning to its original shape upon removal of the load; beyond this, permanent deformation occurs.

qns_content.text: Which type of stress leads to a change in length of a body without changing its shape?

text_solutions: Longitudinal stress (tensile or compressive) causes a change in length along the direction of the applied force without altering the shape of the body.

qns_content.text: Which of the following best defines stress in the context of mechanical properties of solids?

text_solutions: Stress is defined as the restoring force per unit area developed in a body due to an external deforming force, given by \( \text{Stress} = \frac{F}{A} \).

qns_content.text: What does the steepness of the linear portion of a stress-strain curve typically indicate about a material?

text_solutions: The steepness of the linear portion of the stress-strain curve indicates a higher Young’s modulus, meaning the material is stiffer and requires more stress to produce a given strain.

qns_content.text: An aluminium rod of length \( 1.6 \, \text{m} \) and cross-sectional area \( 2 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{m}^2 \) is compressed by a force of \( 600 \, \text{N} \). If the Young's modulus of aluminium is \( 7 \times 10^{10} \, \text{N/m}^2 \), what is the compression?

text_solutions:
Bulk modulus: B = -p / (ΔV / V).

Rearrange: p = -B × (ΔV / V).

Given: ΔV / V = -0.05% = -0.0005.

Substitute: p = 2.2 × 109 × 0.0005 = 1.1 × 106 N/m2.

qns_content.text: A steel wire of length 4 m and cross-sectional area 2 × 10-6 m2 is stretched by 0.4 mm. If the force applied is 200 N, what is the Young's modulus of the steel?

text_solutions:
Young's modulus: Y = (F L) / (A ΔL).

Substitute: ΔL = 0.4 × 10-3 m.

Y = (200 × 4) / (2 × 10-6 × 0.4 × 10-3) = 800 / (8 × 10-10) = 1 × 1012 N/m2.

qns_content.text: A steel wire of length 3 m and cross-sectional area 4 × 10-6 m2 is stretched by 0.3 mm. If the Young's modulus of steel is 2 × 1011 N/m2, what is the force applied?

text_solutions:
Young's modulus: Y = (F L) / (A ΔL).

Rearrange: F = (Y A ΔL) / L.

Substitute: ΔL = 0.3 × 10-3 m, so F = (2 × 1011 × 4 × 10-6 × 0.3 × 10-3) / 3 = 80 N.

qns_content.text: Why is steel often chosen over materials like copper for heavy-duty structural applications?

text_solutions: Steel has a higher Young’s modulus (\( \approx 200 \times 10^9 \, \text{N/m}^2 \)) compared to copper (\( \approx 110 \times 10^9 \, \text{N/m}^2 \)), requiring a larger force to produce the same deformation, making it more suitable for resisting bending and stretching.

text_solutions: The tight coupling between neighboring atoms in solids results in a much higher resistance to volume change compared to gases, where molecules are weakly coupled.

qns_content.text: A copper wire of length 1.5 m and diameter 1 mm is subjected to a tensile force of 100 N. If the Young's modulus of copper is 1.1 × 1011 N/m2, what is the stress in the wire?

Area: A = π r2, r = 1 × 10-3 m.

qns_content.text: A copper block of dimensions 0.4 m × 0.3 m × 0.1 m is subjected to a shearing force of 3 × 104 N. If the shear modulus of copper is 4.2 × 1010 N/m2, what is the displacement of the top face?

Shear modulus: G = (F / A) / (Δx / L).

Rearrange: Δx = (F L) / (A G).

Area: A = 0.4 × 0.3 = 0.12 m2, L = 0.1 m.

Substitute: Δx = (3 × 104 × 0.1) / (0.12 × 4.2 × 1010) = 3000 / (5.04 × 109) ≈ 5.95 × 10-7 m.

Why do engineers prefer materials with a large Young’s modulus for designing columns and beams?

text_solutions: Materials with a large Young’s modulus are stiffer, requiring greater force to produce small deformations, which ensures better resistance to bending and stretching.

Shear modulus: \( G = \frac{\text{Shear stress}}{\text{Shear strain}} \).

Shear stress: \( \text{Shear stress} = \frac{F}{A} \), \( A = 0.3 \times 0.2 = 0.06 \, \text{m}^2 \).
